title: One thrombolysis, two vascular emergencies: A case of concurrent acute ischemic stroke and ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
authors: Ali Eren Ersin; Esma Hande Tural; Eylem TEKE
abstract: Introduction: The simultaneous occurrence of acute ischemic stroke and acute myocardial infarction, described as “cardiocerebral infarction,” is a clinically challenging condition. Although both diseases require urgent reperfusion, there is no common algorithm regarding treatment doses, interventional approaches, and bleeding risk. This report aims to present a patient whose neurological and coronary findings regressed after IV thrombolytic therapy given for acute ischemic stroke.Case: A 66-year-old woman with a history of HTN and DM presented to another center with simultaneous onset of right arm weakness and chest pain. On presentation, right upper extremity muscle strength was 3/5 and NIHSS was 2. Brain CT showed no hemorrhage; diffusion MRI showed diffusion restriction in the bilateral frontal regions. At 2 hours from symptom onset, IV tPA was given with a diagnosis of hyperacute ischemic stroke. Afterward, right upper extremity strength rose to 4/5 and NIHSS fell to 1. The ECG obtained at the same time showed ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, and troponin was 30.9 initially, 724.2 on follow-up, and peaked at 1,300 nanogram/L. She was referred to our center’s coronary intensive care unit with a preliminary diagnosis of ACS. Serial ECGs showed regression of the ST elevations. Transthoracic echo showed EF 50%, basal inferior hypokinesis, grade 2 mitral and aortic regurgitation, LA 39 mm (diameter) and LVH. On coronary angiography the next day, 40% stenosis of the proximal and mid LAD, 30% stenosis of the proximal RCA, and diffuse plaques in the Cx were seen. Percutaneous coronary intervention was not required, and medical follow-up was decided. The patient was then transferred to the neurology ward. In our patient, the regression of chest pain and ST elevations together with neurological improvement after IV tPA given at the stroke dose suggests that the coronary thrombus may have been dissolved by IV tPA. However, spontaneous coronary reperfusion, coronary vasospasm, MINOCA, stress cardiomyopathy, and stroke-related neurogenic myocardial injury should also be considered in the differential diagnosis. The timing of antiplatelet therapy and invasive coronary intervention after thrombolysis should be individualized, taking the risk of intracranial hemorrhage into account (Figure 1–6).Discussion/Conclusion: In patients with acute neurological deficit accompanied by chest pain, cerebral and cardiac evaluation should be carried out together. IV tPA given for acute ischemic stroke may contribute to reperfusion in a concomitant thrombotic coronary occlusion. However, this possibility should be interpreted together with serial ECGs, cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography, and coronary angiography data.Keywords:

title: Edge-to-edge mitral valve repair for bileaflet prolapse in Barlow disease
authors: Nicolò Azzola Guicciardi; Guido Ascione; Alessandro Faggi; P Malvindi; Alessandro Castiglioni; Ottavio Alfieri; Francesco Maisano; Michele De Bonis
abstract: Barlow disease with bileaflet prolapse represents one of the most challenging lesions in degenerative mitral valve surgery. Multiple prolapsing segments, excess leaflet tissue, elongated chordae and annular dilatation often coexist, requiring a comprehensive repair strategy. The edge-to-edge technique, first introduced in 1991, provides a simple and reproducible method to restore leaflet coaptation in this complex setting. By approximating the free edges of the anterior and posterior leaflets at the site of regurgitation, a double-orifice mitral valve is created. This single manoeuvre effectively addresses bileaflet prolapse, reduces leaflet height, forces coaptation, restricts excessive leaflet motion and prevents systolic anterior motion of the anterior leaflet. A concomitant ring annuloplasty is strongly recommended to remodel the dilated annulus, stabilize the repair and ensure long-term durability. This video tutorial presents the key surgical steps of the double-orifice edge-to-edge repair combined with annuloplasty for the treatment of severe mitral regurgitation caused by bileaflet prolapse in Barlow disease. The procedure is performed through a anterolateral minithoracotomy at the fourth intercostal space under video assistance with peripherical cardiopulmonary bypass and cardioplegic arrest. Technical tips for patient selection, suture placement, leaflet assessment, avoidance of mitral stenosis and intraoperative competence testing are provided.

title: Left atrial reservoir strain is independently associated with heart failure hospitalization beyond NT-proBNP in HFpEF with non-paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
authors: Ying Lü; Lei Huang; Xiaohu CHEN; Jianghong Li
abstract: Introduction Patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and non-paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) are at high risk of heart failure hospitalization (HFH). In AF, NT-proBNP interpretation is complicated by rhythm- and load-related factors, motivating markers of atrial mechanics. Left atrial reservoir strain (LASr) reflects atrial mechanical function, compliance, and chronic filling-pressure burden. This study assessed whether LASr was independently associated with first HFH beyond NT-proBNP. Methods We retrospectively identified 432 patients with LVEF ≥50%, HFpEF (chiefly HFA-PEFF; invasive wedge pressure in 78, 18.1%), and non-paroxysmal AF from two centers. LASr was measured offline by two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography on a single vendor platform, with at least five cardiac cycles averaged. The primary endpoint was first HFH. Cox models assessed apparent and bootstrap optimism-corrected performance, with proportional hazards diagnostics and sensitivity analyses including adjustment for left atrial volume index (LAVI) and a high-certainty HFpEF cohort. Results During a median follow-up of 31.7 (24.3–37.8) months, 124 patients (28.7%) reached the endpoint. Baseline LASr was lower in these patients (11.1% vs. 14.8%; P < 0.001). After adjustment for clinical variables, log NT-proBNP, LV GLS, and E/e′, LASr remained independently associated with HFH (HR 0.61 per 1-SD increase, 95% CI: 0.49–0.76, equivalent to HR 1.11 per 1% absolute decrease, 95% CI: 1.06–1.16), and the association persisted after further adjustment for LAVI (HR 0.61, 95% CI: 0.49–0.76). Log NT-proBNP (HR 1.32, 95% CI: 1.04–1.68) and E/e′ (HR 1.23, 95% CI: 1.03–1.47) were also independently associated. Adding LASr raised the apparent Harrell C-index from 0.712 to 0.737 and the optimism-corrected C-index from 0.687 to 0.713 (corrected increment 0.027, 95% CI: −0.001 to 0.044). Discussion In HFpEF with non-paroxysmal AF, LASr was independently associated with first HFH after clinical, biomarker, echocardiographic, and left atrial size adjustment, whereas its incremental discrimination beyond NT-proBNP, LV GLS, E/e′, and clinical variables was modest, with an optimism-corrected confidence interval that included zero. This study therefore concludes that lower LASr marks a higher risk of HFH in this population and may complement NT-proBNP, although these retrospective two-center findings, obtained without vital status data, require prospective multicenter validation.

title: Clinical, hematologic, and electrocardiographic factors associated with in-hospital mortality and pre-admission functional status in acute decompensated HFrEF: a retrospective cohort study
authors: Mohammad Taghi Imani; Arzhang Naseri; Nasim Kheirandish; Amir Hossein Imani; Alireza Keshtkar; Elnaz Zare; Mehdi Bazrafshan; Shahrokh Sadeghi Boogar; Ehsan Shojaeefard; Hamed Bazrafshan Drissi
abstract: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) carries substantial short-term risk. We evaluated routinely available clinical, hematologic, and electrocardiographic factors associated with in-hospital mortality and severe pre-admission functional limitation. This retrospective cohort included 100 adults hospitalized with ADHF and HFrEF. In-hospital death was the primary outcome. Because 16 deaths occurred, mortality associations were estimated using a three-variable Firth penalized logistic model including elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), white blood cell (WBC) count, and Bazett-corrected QTc. Model discrimination, calibration, Brier score, and 1,000-resample bootstrap internal validation were assessed. Severe pre-admission functional limitation was analyzed as NYHA class IV versus classes II–III using a separate three-variable binary logistic model. Broad univariable analyses were exploratory and were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate procedure. Sixteen patients (16%) died during hospitalization and 45 had NYHA class IV before admission. Elevated JVP (OR 5.19, 95% profile penalized-likelihood CI 1.23–22.31; p = 0.026), higher WBC count (OR 1.27 per 1 × 10 9 /L, 95% CI 1.04–1.62; p = 0.013), and longer QTc (OR 1.18 per 10 ms, 95% CI 1.04–1.36; p = 0.009) were associated with in-hospital mortality. The apparent AUC was 0.819 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.677–0.933) and the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.794; the corrected calibration slope was 0.953 and Brier score 0.114. NYHA class IV was associated with abnormal lung sounds (OR 4.44, 95% CI 1.44–13.65; p = 0.009), a tricuspid/mitral regurgitation murmur (OR 3.21, 95% CI 1.30–7.93; p = 0.012), and lower alkaline phosphatase (OR 0.58 per 100 U/L increase, 95% CI 0.39–0.87; p = 0.008). No exploratory univariable association remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction. In this small single-center cohort, JVP, WBC count, and QTc showed adjusted associations with in-hospital mortality, while pulmonary findings, valvular murmurs, and alkaline phosphatase were associated with severe pre-admission functional limitation. External validation is required before clinical use.

title: Emergency Physician-Performed Point-of-Care Ultrasound Identified Left Atrial Myxoma in Acute Cerebellar Infarction
authors: Takanobu Sato; Ryo Ichibayashi; Sota Sadamoto
abstract: Cardiac myxoma is a rare but potentially curable cause of cardioembolic stroke. Early identification of a potential cardiac embolic source may be challenging when neurological symptoms predominate during the initial emergency department evaluation. A 72-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute-onset dizziness and vomiting. Although her National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score was 0, she was unable to walk independently. Electrocardiography demonstrated newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation. Because a cardioembolic mechanism was considered, the emergency physician performed bedside cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), which revealed a highly mobile left atrial mass attached to the interatrial septum. POCUS was performed 28 min after arrival, before brain magnetic resonance imaging, which demonstrated multiple acute cerebellar infarctions without large-vessel occlusion. Intravenous alteplase was not administered despite presentation within the therapeutic time window. Anticoagulation with intravenous unfractionated heparin was initiated. Surgical resection was postponed after hemorrhagic transformation of the cerebellar infarction was detected on hospital day 14. The patient underwent complete tumor resection on hospital day 41, and histopathological examination confirmed cardiac myxoma. She was discharged on hospital day 54 with a favorable outcome. This case illustrates the potential value of emergency physician-performed cardiac POCUS for early identification of structural cardiac abnormalities during the initial evaluation of selected patients with suspected cardioembolic stroke.

title: Dual-Valve Infective Endocarditis Caused by Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii in a Patient with Bicuspid Aortic Valve: A Case Report
authors: Huangkan Zhao; Shuchun Wang; Di Wu; Zhaolong Cao; Yuhui Zhang
abstract: Abstract Background Infective endocarditis (IE) caused by carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) is rare and associated with substantial mortality. When it arises on a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), simultaneously involves the aortic and mitral valves, and presents with persistently negative blood cultures, diagnosis and management become exceptionally challenging. Case presentation A 52-year-old man presented with a four-month history of fever and positive rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies, initially raising suspicion of rheumatoid arthritis. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a BAV (right–left cusp fusion), a large mitral anterior leaflet vegetation (1.5 × 1.3 cm), and aortic valve vegetations. Splenic and cerebral infarctions were subsequently identified. Blood cultures remained repeatedly negative in the context of antecedent antimicrobial exposure. He underwent double mechanical valve replacement with vegetation debridement, and intraoperative valve tissue culture grew CRAB, prompting adjustment to a high-dose sulbactam-based regimen. He recovered and was discharged. To our knowledge, this combination of culture-negative CRAB native-valve IE, BAV, dual-valve involvement, and diagnosis solely by intraoperative tissue culture has not previously been reported. This case illustrates a plausible anatomical mechanism linking BAV to concomitant aortic–mitral involvement, highlights the diagnostic value of intraoperative tissue culture and the importance of timely surgical evaluation, and underscores the potential for positive rheumatoid serology to complicate the diagnostic process.

title: Factors Associated With Postoperative High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin T Elevation After Thoracic Surgery: A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study
authors: Ziyi Wang; Wei Zheng; Weijiang Huang; Qi Hu; Lei Pan; Zhimin Liao
abstract: AIM: To examine perioperative factors associated with postoperative high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) elevation after thoracic surgery. METHODS: This single-centre retrospective cohort study screened 588 consecutive records of patients who underwent thoracic surgery between June 2020 and June 2023, counting only the first eligible operation for each patient. After the exclusion of 128 records, all 460 eligible patients were included in the analysis. The outcome was defined as any hs-cTnT value ≥0.014 µg/L (14 ng/L) on postoperative day 1, 3, or 5. Eleven variables were entered simultaneously into a binary logistic regression model, with surgical method represented by indicator variables. Age was entered in years, and its odds ratio (OR) was expressed per 10-year increase; other continuous variables were analysed in their original units. RESULTS: Postoperative hs-cTnT elevation occurred in 155 of 460 patients (33.7%). In the multivariable model, age (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.23–2.63), procedure type (wedge resection: OR 4.47, 95% CI 1.57–12.71; segmentectomy/lobectomy: OR 5.52, 95% CI 2.04–14.96; oesophageal surgery: OR 27.96, 95% CI 5.50–142.27; each compared with other thoracic procedures), operation duration (OR 1.53 per hour, 95% CI 1.21–1.93), preoperative creatinine (OR 1.021 per µmol/L, 95% CI 1.007–1.035), preoperative potassium (OR 3.59 per mmol/L, 95% CI 1.84–7.02), and pre-existing atrial fibrillation (OR 5.56, 95% CI 1.84–16.83) were associated with the outcome. Postoperative day-1 haemoglobin showed an inverse association that did not reach statistical significance (OR 0.972 per g/L, 95% CI 0.942–1.002; p = 0.069), and the inverse association with ejection fraction was also not significant (OR 0.905 per %, 95% CI 0.772–1.060; p = 0.216). CONCLUSIONS: Older age, procedure type, longer operation duration, higher preoperative creatinine, higher preoperative potassium, and pre-existing atrial fibrillation were associated with postoperative hs-cTnT elevation after multivariable adjustment. These associations do not establish causality or constitute a validated prediction model; rather, they generate hypotheses for the prospective evaluation of postoperative monitoring strategies.

title: Experiencia retrospectiva mexicana en el cierre transcatéter de defectos del tabique auricular utilizando diferentes dispositivos
authors: Roberto Mijangos‐Vázquez; Rogelio Hernández-Reyes; Victor M. Pérez-Ruíz
abstract: Background: Over the past decades, significant advancements and innovations have occurred in the field of percutaneous atrial septal defect (ASD) closure using transcatheter-based devices. The Amplatzer septal occluder has been widely used since its Food and Drug Administration approval in 2001. Studies have shown its high success rate in closing ASDs. Since then, many other devices have been developed and used with high technical success and closure rates, with low rates of serious adverse events and device-related complications. When compared to surgery, percutaneous closure provides a less invasive approach with quicker recovery and reduced physical and psychological impact. Objectives: To demonstrate the effectiveness of using different devices for transcatheter ASD closure, emphasizing the success and complications obtained in our patients. Methods: Patients with congenital ASDs who underwent transcatheter closure using different devices were included. The primary endpoint was to determine the efficacy and safety of these devices and to determine the incidence of complications at follow-up. Two hundred and eighty-seven patients underwent ASD closure at a median age of 6 years (7 months-70 years). Results: Only minor complications occurred during catheterization. After a follow-up of 90 ± 67.7 months (up to 96 months), the closure rate was 98.6%, and the absence of atrioventricular block was 100%. Conclusions: Transcatheter ASD closure using percutaneous devices has proven to be safe and effective in most cases. However, careful patient selection and follow-up are necessary to minimize complications and ensure optimal outcomes.

title: Arrhythmia management in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy
authors: Ahmed Yassin; Denise Faro; Peter van der Meer; Yuri Blaauw
abstract: Arrhythmias are common in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and contribute substantially to morbidity at all disease stages. The arrhythmogenic substrate-reflecting diffuse amyloid infiltration, atrial myopathy, autonomic dysfunction, and conduction system involvement-differs fundamentally from that in other cardiomyopathies. Prospective rhythm monitoring reveals a burden substantially higher than previously recognised and predominantly asymptomatic, with bradyarrhythmias and atrial fibrillation (AF) dominating and sustained ventricular arrhythmias remaining rare.This review examines key aspects of arrhythmia management in ATTR-CM. Conduction system disease is frequently encountered, and pacing strategies-including conduction system pacing-are discussed in the context of progressive infiltrative disease. We address the rationale for lifelong anticoagulation in AF irrespective of CHA2DS2-VA-score, and emerging considerations for anticoagulation in selected sinus rhythm patients with impaired atrial function. Rhythm control strategies are reviewed in light of extensive atrial substrate, high AF recurrence rates, and the absence of randomised trial data. The role of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators is examined, with emphasis on the lack of proven survival benefit for primary prevention. Finally, we explore disease-modifying therapies and their potential to attenuate the arrhythmogenic substrate. Overall, structured surveillance, rhythm control, and individualised device decisions form the cornerstones of modern arrhythmia management in ATTR-CM.

title: MANAGEMENT OF ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE IN A 12-YEAR-OLD BOY WITH CHRONIC RHEUMATIC MULTIVALVULAR HEART DISEASE AND SEVERE PERICARDIAL EFFUSION: A CASE REPORT
authors: Nastiti Hasnawati; Ayu Diah Perdana Paramita; Rosi Indah Pratama
journal: The International Journal of Medical Science and Health Research
abstract: Introduction: Acute heart failure (AHF) in children is a life-threatening clinical syndrome whose aetiological spectrum differs markedly between high-income and low- and middle-income countries. In Indonesia and other endemic regions, chronic rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a leading acquired cause of paediatric heart failure, frequently presenting late with advanced multivalvular disease, ventricular dysfunction and pericardial involvement. Early recognition, haemodynamic stabilisation and timely referral are decisive for survival, particularly in district hospitals with limited diagnostic resources. Case Illustration: A 12-year-old boy presented with progressively worsening dyspnoea for three days, accompanied by cough, bilateral leg oedema, orthopnoea and palpitations, on a background of intermittent dyspnoea for one year. Thirteen months earlier, an outside M-mode echocardiogram had documented left-sided chamber enlargement, a reduced ejection fraction (27.5%), mild pericardial effusion and suspected RHD. On admission he had diaphoresis at rest, scleral icterus, tachycardia, a cardiac murmur with gallop rhythm, tachypnoea, rhonchi and wheezing, hepatomegaly, ascites and pedal oedema, yielding a modified Ross score of 11 (severe heart failure). Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia, right axis deviation, biatrial enlargement, prolonged PR interval (197 ms), Q waves in the high lateral leads and electrical alternans; chest radiography demonstrated marked cardiomegaly. He received inotropic support with dobutamine and dopamine together with furosemide and spironolactone, and improved clinically. After stabilisation he was referred through the outpatient clinic to the provincial referral hospital, where echocardiography confirmed chronic RHD with mitral, tricuspid and aortic regurgitation and a severe pericardial effusion. He was hospitalised for approximately seven days under a paediatric cardiology consultant, recovered, and was discharged home with long-term follow-up. Discussion: This case illustrates the typical late presentation of RHD in an endemic setting, the pathophysiological interplay of chronic volume overload, ventricular dysfunction and pericardial effusion, and the practical value of bedside severity scoring, electrocardiography and radiography where echocardiography is not immediately available. Inotropes combined with loop diuretics and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist achieved decongestion, while the severe pericardial effusion mandated exclusion of tamponade physiology before aggressive preload reduction. The missed opportunity 13 months earlier underscores the importance of registry-based follow-up, secondary antibiotic prophylaxis tailored to cardiovascular risk, and early referral for definitive valve intervention. Conclusion: Paediatric AHF due to chronic RHD can be stabilised successfully at district level through structured clinical assessment, judicious inotropic and diuretic therapy and prompt referral. Long-term outcome depends on secondary prophylaxis, guideline-directed heart failure therapy, nutritional rehabilitation and access to surgical valve repair.

title: Sustained Ventricular Tachycardia Revealing Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy With Severe Ventricular Electrical Instability: A Case Report
authors: Ayoub Laaboussi; Nada Douari; Wassim Beladel; Amine El Houari; Khalil Abderrahmane Elbaz; Mohamed El Minaoui
abstract: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is an inherited cardiomyopathy characterized by fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.Sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) may be the first manifestation of the disease, and left ventricular involvement is increasingly recognized.A 53-year-old man, followed for approximately 10 years for an incompletely characterized cardiomyopathy associated with palpitations, was admitted for sustained VT with a left bundle branch block morphology and an inferior axis, suggesting a right ventricular origin.The arrhythmia was successfully terminated by intravenous amiodarone.Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a dilated and hypertrophied right ventricle with an apical aneurysm and prominent free-wall trabeculations, severe right ventricular systolic dysfunction (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion of 11 mm, systolic tricuspid annular velocity of 7 cm/s, fractional area change of 23%, and free-wall longitudinal strain of -10.5%), as well as concomitant moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction of 43%).Cardiac MRI demonstrated mid-apical right ventricular free-wall dyskinesia, an indexed right ventricular end-diastolic volume of 145.28 mL/m², a right ventricular ejection fraction of 23%, and late gadolinium enhancement of the right ventricular free wall.Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries.Prolonged ambulatory ECG monitoring revealed marked ventricular instability, with 169,148 ventricular premature beats over approximately three days, including three predominant morphologies, 31,972 couplets, and 13,863 ventricular runs, and 161 episodes of ventricular tachyarrhythmia, comprising approximately 20 episodes of non-sustained VT, with the remaining episodes corresponding to accelerated idioventricular rhythm.Bradycardia developed during treatment with amiodarone and a beta-blocker, requiring dose reduction.The diagnosis of definite ARVC was established based on the diagnostic criteria.A dual-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was subsequently implanted for secondary prevention.Amiodarone was discontinued after implantation because of persistent bradycardia.The subsequent clinical course was favorable, with no recurrent symptoms or documented arrhythmic events during the available follow-up.This case illustrates the revelation of ARVC by sustained VT, the central role of multimodality imaging in establishing the diagnosis, the importance of arrhythmic risk stratification for secondary-prevention defibrillator therapy, and the need to adapt antiarrhythmic treatment to arrhythmic burden and hemodynamic tolerance.

title: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair for post-myocardial infarction papillary muscle rupture: a systematic review of patient-level and aggregate outcomes
authors: Darpan Kothia; Lillian Short; Asaad Mouselli; Chirag Lodha; Erica Thomson; Rohit R. Amin
abstract: Papillary muscle rupture (PMR) is a rare mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) that causes acute severe mitral regurgitation (MR), pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock. Surgery remains standard therapy, but many patients are prohibitive surgical risk. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) has emerged as a rescue option, although reported outcomes are vulnerable to selection and publication bias. We performed a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Eligible reports described TEER for acute severe MR caused by definite papillary muscle rupture or papillary muscle tear attributable to AMI or acute myocardial ischemia. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts and independently extracted data using a standardized form; disagreements were resolved by consensus, with senior-author adjudication when required. Aggregate series and registry data were analyzed separately to avoid duplicate counting. Thirty-one eligible reports were identified. After accounting for one overlapping companion case report within a later aggregate series, the primary non-overlapping synthesis comprised 55 unique patients: 27 patients from selected individual reports and 28 patients from three consecutive or multicenter series. Among individual reports with available data, cardiogenic shock or other critical illness was documented in 24/24, and temporary circulatory or respiratory support was used in 19/21. Survival to hospital discharge was 27/27 (100%) in selected individual reports versus 19/28 (67.9%) in consecutive/multicenter series. This 32.1-percentage-point difference is consistent with substantial publication and selection bias but may also reflect differences in case mix, anatomy, procedural era, device generation, and center experience. IREMMI registry data showed similar discharge survival in a less-selected population. TEER is technically feasible as a rescue strategy for selected patients with post-AMI PMR when emergency surgery is prohibitive, but the available evidence does not establish comparative efficacy or survival benefit. Outcomes from isolated case reports are substantially more favorable than outcomes from consecutive series. TEER is best framed as emergency stabilization and a bridge to reassessment, with delayed surgery as one possible subsequent pathway. Consecutive multicenter registries and standardized reporting are needed. This review was not prospectively registered (see Methods, Design and registration).

title: Case Report: Coronary artery involvement and nonvisualization of pulmonary artery branches first detected during follow-up of Takayasu arteritis
authors: Maiqi Liu; Haohu Wu; 侯岩峰
abstract: Takayasu arteritis (TA) is a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of unknown etiology that can involve the coronary and pulmonary arteries. A 30-year-old woman presented with crushing chest pain and was found to have 95% stenosis at the ostium of the left main coronary artery. Approximately 3.5 months after coronary stent implantation, severe in-stent restenosis occurred, requiring balloon angioplasty. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed thickening of the ascending aorta and aortic arch wall with increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake, supporting the clinical diagnosis of TA. She received glucocorticoids and methotrexate and, because of persistent coronary disease, underwent off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting, followed by tocilizumab. During follow-up, C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate remained within reference ranges. In September 2025, echocardiography estimated a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 21 mmHg, whereas an October examination did not report pulmonary hypertension. On October 15, 2025, right heart catheterization measured a pulmonary artery pressure of 39/10 mmHg (mean 20 mmHg), which did not meet the current hemodynamic threshold for pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary angiography showed nonvisualization of the right upper and middle lobar pulmonary artery branches. Because of the lack of baseline pulmonary vascular imaging or a complete evaluation of alternative causes, the onset and etiology of this finding remain uncertain. Normal acute-phase reactants during tocilizumab therapy should not be regarded as evidence of the absence of vascular disease, and angiographic nonvisualization alone cannot establish active vasculitic occlusion.
